items.summary: arXiv:2611.28508v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Understanding naturalistic brain activity requires going beyond the stimulus alone, as external inputs continuously interact with an individual's evolving brain state. A world model captures such dynamics in a latent state by inferring it from neural observations, predicting stimulus-driven evolution, and updating with new observations. However, existing brain world models fail to maintain a persistent latent state over time, and standard metrics of neural prediction accuracy cannot tell whether a model tracks an individual's brain state or relies solely on the stimulus. To directly test state inference, prediction, and updating, we introduce BrainStateBench, which evaluates a model's latent state through a frozen linear probe on whole-cortex, movie-driven fMRI. Its State task tests whether a model captures trial-to-trial variability in an individual's responses to repeated stimuli, while Forecast and Updating evaluate future activity predictions without and with new observations, respectively. To track individual brain state across time, we propose Spectator, a linear latent world model trained with a joint-embedding predictive objective. Spectator encodes short- and long-horizon observation histories into a two-timescale latent state and predicts state transitions linearly from the current state and stimulus. Stimulus-only encoders reach 0.320 in fMRI prediction correlation without observing the brain (0% on State), while prior deep brain world models reach 0.239 yet score at most 0.4% on State. In contrast, Spectator achieves 0.349 correlation alongside 5.5% on State, 16.0% on Forecast, and 20.3% on Updating, outperforming all baselines while forecasting over 20x faster than deep forecasting models.

items.title: DisSparse: Pipelined Top-$p$ Sparse Attention for Long-Context LLM Serving
items.summary: arXiv:2611.28522v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long-context LLM inference is bottlenecked by the memory demands of the key-value (KV) cache, whose size scales linearly with context length. Dynamic sparse attention reduces this bottleneck by fetching and attending only to a critical subset of tokens. The dominant primitive in dynamic sparse attention research and deployment is fixed-budget top-$k$ selection, which is favored because its deterministic block count aligns with the static memory allocation that systems like vLLM rely on. Top-$k$ uses a fixed budget regardless of how attention mass is distributed across heads, layers, and decode steps, leading to either wasted bandwidth on heads with peaky attention or dropped context on heads with diffuse attention. Top-$p$ (nucleus) selection adapts naturally to this variation but has seen limited adoption in production serving systems due to two system-level challenges: variable block counts that break deterministic block allocation and computationally expensive selection kernels that exceed the cost of attention itself. We present DisSparse, a serving system that integrates top-$p$ sparse attention into vLLM end-to-end. DisSparse decouples block selection from the scheduler's critical path, hides selection latency behind layer computation via a two-stream pipeline, and introduces a single-pass histogram-based top-$p$ kernel. We further observe intra-block sparsity, the inflation of selection budgets caused by mixing high- and low-importance tokens within fixed-size KV cache blocks, and address it with a token relocation kernel guided by accumulated prefill attention scores. Across long- and medium-context benchmarks on multiple models, DisSparse achieves 1.17x to 1.80x speedup in sparsity analysis (block selection) over state-of-the-art top-$p$ methods with negligible accuracy loss and supports up to 8x larger maximum batch sizes than dense vLLM under the same memory budget.

items.title: SAFE-DRIFT: Data Selection for Supervised Fine-tuning with Controllable Off-Target Drifts
items.summary: arXiv:2611.28560v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose SAFE-DRIFT, a data-selection framework for supervised fine-tuning that improves a target capability while controlling unwanted drift in the model's other behaviors. We formalize this as a constrained optimization problem that maximizes alignment with the target gradient, subject to a budget on off-target drift which we quantify using the Fisher information of a reference distribution. Under this objective, the optimal, closed-form update is a damped natural-gradient step that downweights reference-sensitive directions. To estimate these high-dimensional gradients and work within the right geometry, we further derive a scalable algorithm that approximates the Fisher information and the target gradient in a shared low-dimensional subspace and analyze how entanglement of the target and reference task can affect the update. We evaluate SAFE-DRIFT against state-of-the-art data selection methods across diverse domains including coding and medical question answering, yielding competitive target performance while reducing degradation on specified off-target behaviors.

items.title: Tight Mistake-Abstention Tradeoffs for Sequential Prediction under Adversarial Injections
items.summary: arXiv:2611.28579v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the sequential prediction problem introduced by Goel et al. (2023), where an adversary can inject arbitrarily many corrupted instances in an i.i.d. stream from a clean distribution $\mu$, while the learner is allowed to abstain from making a prediction at no cost if the current instance was indeed injected. When $\mu$ is unknown, Yu and Blanchard (2026) show a polynomial tradeoff between mistakes and false abstentions for classes with finite VC dimension and oblivious adversaries, but still leave open a significant gap between upper and lower bounds in their tradeoff landscape. In this paper, we propose the weighted shattering potential, and based on variants of this potential, provide gap-closing algorithms that essentially characterize the tradeoffs under various settings of interest: When $\mu$ is known, our algorithm improves over Goel et al. (2023) and achieves their conjectured $O(d\log T)$ mistake bound; When $\mu$ is unknown, for oblivious adversary, our guarantees are tight both in $T$ and in terms of the VC dimension $d$, which completely characterizes the abstention-mistake tradeoff in this setting and gives an $O(\sqrt{dT})$ balanced rate. For adaptive adversary, our results are tight up to $\operatorname{poly}(dD\log T)$ factors for structured classes with finite so-called reduction dimension $D$. Our guarantees also extend to censored feedback, where the label is hidden after an abstention.

items.title: Understanding and Mitigating the Fragility of Self-Rewarding Optimization
items.summary: arXiv:2611.28582v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Self-rewarding optimization (SRO) promises to improve language models by enabling them to generate their own reward signals. Yet when and how SRO succeeds or fails remains poorly understood. We reveal that SRO is fundamentally fragile: even seemingly benign perturbations to training prompts can corrupt the self-generated preference signal and trigger iterative collapse. We demonstrate this through two prompt-level attacks that serve as controlled stress tests: a Re-Ranking attack that concentrates training on prompts where self-reward diverges from an oracle, and a Preamble attack that learns short prefixes inflating self-reward without any gain in oracle quality. To explain why these attacks succeed, we introduce self-reward fidelity (SRF), a metric quantifying on-policy agreement between self-evaluated and oracle rewards. We show that SRF can serve as a diagnostic signal of self-supervision reliability, and that controlled SRF perturbations induce a phase-transition region: SRO improves when SRF remains sufficiently high, but collapses once SRF drops below a model- and task-dependent threshold. This analysis motivates Projection Decoupling Defense, which suppresses SRO update components along directions to which the reward generator is locally sensitive, improving SRO robustness under adversarial conditions. This work sheds light on the fragility of SRO and charts promising directions toward making it more robust.

items.title: DRAM: Memory-Efficient Muon via Rank Reallocation in Principal-Random Subspaces
items.summary: arXiv:2611.28595v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Memory-efficient Muon methods aim to reduce storage overhead while preserving strong performance, yet existing approaches compromise either convergence guarantees or practical efficiency. In this paper, we focus on subspace optimization for Muon, where the choice of subspace determines the gradient information retained for updating. To preserve dominant information while providing the coverage needed for stochastic convergence guarantees, we construct a principal-random subspace that combines leading singular directions of the stochastic gradient with random directions sampled from their orthogonal complement. Under a fixed rank budget, there is a trade-off between principal exploitation and complementary coverage, making rank allocation important for practical optimization. Our key observation is that the preferred balance shifts from principal-heavy early in training to random-heavy later. Motivated by this shift, we propose \dram, a memory-efficient Muon optimizer that reallocates principal and random ranks across stages while maintaining momentum and performing matrix-sign normalization entirely in the subspace. Theoretically, we establish convergence guarantees for general rank-allocation schedules with nondecreasing coverage factors, obtaining rates of $O(T^{-1/4})$ in the stochastic setting and $O(T^{-1/2})$ in the deterministic setting, with fixed allocation as a special case. Using a simple linear reallocation schedule, \dram achieves the best low-memory performance across three pre-training scales and nine fine-tuning settings.

items.title: Bridging Teacher-Student Capability Gaps with Recurrent Computation
items.summary: arXiv:2611.28603v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Knowledge distillation transfers capabilities from large language models to smaller students, yet stronger teachers do not always yield better students. Recent studies report diminishing or even negative returns from teacher scaling. We hypothesize that these limitations arise in part from insufficient student capacity to absorb the teacher's knowledge. We therefore investigate loop and recurrent computation as a way to expand the student's effective capacity by modifying its computation graph while keeping the backbone parameter count fixed. Under teacher-forced KD during pretraining, weight-shared looping improves performance but retains teacher-size saturation, whereas cross-token recurrence avoids the observed reversal with larger teachers. In mathematical post-training under both teacher-forced KD and on-policy distillation (OPD), recurrent students scale better with increasing teacher size than looped and vanilla LLMs do. Crucially, we show that a pretrained LLM can be readily fine-tuned into a looped or recurrent architecture jointly with OPD, without repeating pretraining. Our recurrent Qwen model improves with larger teachers and consistently outperforms looped and vanilla LLMs. This suggests a new post-training paradigm that integrates architectural conversion into distillation, avoiding a separate conversion stage while substantially improving student performance and maintaining near-vanilla inference latency.

items.title: BitShare: Sensitivity-Aware Binning and Bit Sharing for Compacting LLM Weight Storage
items.summary: arXiv:2611.28607v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Decoding with large language models at small batch sizes is limited by memory bandwidth, so the bits stored per weight largely set its cost. Group-wise integer quantization stores every weight of a group at the same precision, although the input channels of a group differ in sensitivity. We present BITSHARE, a codebook-free weight format that keeps the integer grid and the dequantizer of group-wise quantization but varies precision within each group. Sensitivity-aware binning places the channels of each group into three bins at fixed positions, and static bit sharing with optimal bit-value allocation lets the less sensitive weights share their lower bits, each stored once per group or once per pair of weights. A sharing-aware version of GPTQ chooses every stored value, with no fine-tuning and no codebook. BITSHARE has two modes. BITSHARE-U gives every group the same layout, so its decoder routes bits by fixed wiring, while BITSHARE-N chooses a layout per group within the same bit budget. With calibration on the Pile and at the same storage, both modes have lower perplexity than GPTQ at 3 and 2 bits on WikiText-2 and C4. At 2 bits across Llama-2 and Llama-3 models, BITSHARE-N lowers WikiText-2 perplexity by up to 70% against SliM-LLM and up to 35% against GPTAQ. At the 2-bit perplexity of SliM-LLM, BITSHARE-U stores 13.6-19.4% fewer bits per weight, cutting DRAM weight traffic by the same fraction. A verified hardware decoder implementation synthesized in SkyWater 130 nm reconstructs BITSHARE weights at the throughput of INT-n and SliM-LLM decoders.

items.title: Action-Conditioned Transition Irreversibility for Out-of-Distribution Detection in Reinforcement Learning
items.summary: arXiv:2611.28611v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement-learning agents shape the observations they encounter; consequently, detecting out-of-distribution (OOD) states requires analysing action-conditioned trajectories rather than treating inputs as independent samples. We propose Action-Conditioned Transition Irreversibility (ACTI), a detector that evaluates forward and backward transition likelihoods, calibrates this comparison against the in-distribution profile at each timestep, and smooths the score over a short window, using no future information. We tested ACTI across six environments and fifteen detectors within OOD-RL-Bench, using the four anomaly mechanisms that qualified in every environment, with ten policy replicates per environment. All primary metrics are matched-time: each score after anomaly onset is compared with a clean twin rollout's score at the same timestep. Our method secured the top macro matched-time AUROC, outperforming the dynamics-model baseline (PEDM), while scoring transitions roughly two orders of magnitude faster. Compared to the state-only variant, ACTI achieved a small but consistent AUROC gain and a shorter detection delay. The capacity-matched forward-only baseline, ACTI-Forward, secured a statistically significant advantage in AUPRC alongside a reduced detection delay. The discrepancy in AUROC did not reach statistical significance. Ablation studies suggest instead that performance improvements stem from action conditioning, calibration at each timestep, and smoothing of the transition-likelihood scores. Based on these results, we recommend using ACTI-Forward.

items.title: Interpreting Diffusion Model Activations in Natural Language
items.summary: arXiv:2611.28621v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Interpreting the intermediate activations of diffusion models (DMs) is key to understanding how they generate images. Existing interpretability methods for DMs provide limited support for open-ended interrogation, making it difficult to extract human-interpretable insights. We extend LatentQA, the task of answering natural-language questions about Large Language Model activations, to DM activations. We introduce the Diffusion-specific Activation Oracle (DAO), which translates DM activations into natural-language answers to open-ended questions about the ongoing generation. Our experiments show that DAO can effectively describe the content of the final image from activations at early denoising steps. Additionally, we demonstrate that DAO captures the structure of the DM's activation space well enough to steer image generation toward target attributes. Furthermore, we show that attribution patching through DAO identifies DM components that contribute to visual attributes specified in natural language. Our code is available \href{https://github.com/yamanoko/dao/tree/main}{here}.

items.title: Nearly Minimax-Optimal Sample Complexity of Natural Policy Gradient with a Matching Information-Theoretic Lower Bound
items.summary: arXiv:2611.28628v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A fundamental question in reinforcement learning is how many sampled transitions are needed to learn a near-optimal policy, and whether direct policy optimization can attain this statistical limit. To answer this question, we consider natural policy gradient (NPG), a widely used policy optimization method. We study tabular finite-horizon Markov decision processes (MDPs) with known rewards and unknown horizon-dependent transition kernels, accessed through a generative model. Our sample-based NPG algorithms update the policy by backward sweeps and do not estimate transition probabilities. Under three different batch-size and step size schedules, we establish last-iterate guarantees with sample complexity $\widetilde O(SAH^4/\varepsilon^2)$, where $S$, $A$, and $H$ denote the number of states, the number of actions, and the horizon length, respectively. In this setting, horizon-dependent transition kernels contribute a factor of $H$ to our transition-query bound. Our information-theoretic lower bound of $\Omega(SAH^4/\varepsilon^2)$ shows that the resulting $H^4$ dependence is unavoidable in the worst case, even for agents that select their queries adaptively. To the best of our knowledge, these are the first last-iterate guarantees for NPG whose sample complexity matches an information-theoretic lower bound up to logarithmic factors. Consequently, our results demonstrate that direct policy-space optimization through NPG can achieve the fundamental statistical limits of reinforcement learning while guaranteeing the performance of the final policy. Furthermore, for known kernels, we prove that exact NPG with a constant step size $\eta=1/H$ requires $\Omega(H^2/\varepsilon)$ iterations in the worst case, matching the known upper bound for that step size.

items.title: Show HN: Mason – a lightweight Postgres read-replica, built on columnar storage
items.summary: Hi HN! TLDR: we’ve built an open-source drop-in replacement for a postgres read-replica, powered by duckdb’s columnar compute engine. It’s very fast. And it looks like postgres. So, this started out as: let’s just connect Clickhouse to our postgres dbs and throw our analytics queries at it instead. That will speed everything up. But we quickly found that 1) Clickhouse comes with quite the learning curve (engine optimisation) to make it fast (we needed something we could easily drop in to any customer’s postgres scenario), and 2) we had underestimated how different clickhouse’s SQL syntax was to postgres. Don’t get me wrong: we love Clickhouse (it’s ridiculously fast if you know what queries to expect), it just didn’t work for our ad-hoc postgres workloads. So we went searching for alternatives that were 1) more plug-and-play and 2) looked a lot more like postgres. We dismissed a bunch based on desk research alone: - pg_mooncake (seems to have stalled since data bricks bought them) - pg_duckdb (seems to offer fast queries, or fresh data, but not both - we needed both) - materialize/risingwave/readyset (like Clickhouse, they require knowing the query shapes upfront - not ideal for ad-hoc workloads) - firebolt (license makes it challenging to offer to our customers) - redshift / alloydb / etc (we wanted something cloud-provider agnostic) And we shortlisted 3: - pg_clickhouse (Postgres extension that parses SQL in Postgres and pushes the work down to ClickHouse) - cedarDB (closed-source, Postgres-compatible analytical database) - duckdb (open-source, embedded columnar analytics engine with a Postgres-like SQL dialect) We needed to know how they would perform on real postgres queries, so we took a backlog of 5,410 (hand-written) queries (chosen because they had been slow to execute against postgres) from 159 real postgres databases. We then generated synthetic data (dynamically using the schemas from those 159 databases) to fill 159 local databases so we could run the experiment. We then spun up the 3 short-listed tools locally, and ran each of the 5,410 queries against both postgres and the 3 tools, and compared the results: - pg_clickhouse (matched postgres 59.4% of the time, refused 39.9% of the queries and was “wrong” 0.8% of the time). - cedarDB (matched postgres 88.1% of the time, refused 8% of the queries and was “wrong” 3.9% of the time). - duckdb (matched postgres 84.1% of the time, refused 14.3% of the queries and was “wrong” 1.6% of the time). Matched meant they returned exactly the same result as postgres. Refused meant they returned an error message (usually telling you some syntax isn’t recognised). And “wrong” meant they didn’t return the same results as postgres. I appreciate that arguably postgres may be the one that is wrong in some cases - but for our use case, we considered postgres the golden source of truth. So, both duckdb and cedardb performed pretty well (correctly handled more than 80% of the postgres queries we threw at it), out-of-the box. But we really still wanted to try and cover that long-tail. We chose duckdb as its open-source license would allow us to easily work on the long tail to get the postgres SQL parity we wanted. So, Mason (linked above), is what we built, powered by duckdb, which now matches postgres on 96% of our 5,410 queries, plus hundreds of other queries that we added, testing it with Metabase, Grafana, Superset, DBeaver and Trevor.io. For the remaining 4%, it errors with a nice clear message telling you how to rewrite your SQL. We’d love your feedback on what we’ve built. Useful? How can we make it better?
